title: Routine Operator Care versus Skilled Maintenance

content.overview: Operator care supports reliable equipment, but the technician must stop where routine cleaning and inspection become servicing, disassembly or hazardous-energy work.

vocabulary.definition: Routine cleaning, observation, setup and simple maintenance activities explicitly assigned to the equipment operator.
Work on equipment that may involve adjustment, repair, jam clearing, replacement or other activities that can create exposure to hazards.
Electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal, gravitational or other energy that can injure workers if unexpectedly released.

sections.title: Operator care is explicitly defined
sections.body: Routine care can include accessible cleaning, external observations and simple checks only when the equipment instructions and facility SOP assign them to the operator. The technician does not expand the task because a repair appears simple.

sections.title: Servicing changes the risk
sections.body: Opening guards, entering machinery, clearing jams, accessing electrical components or other covered servicing can expose workers to hazardous energy. OSHA 1910.147 provides the general-industry energy-control framework for covered servicing and maintenance; Technician I does not confer authorization for such work.

workedExamples: An operator performs the approved external emitter check but escalates a blockage that requires disassembly.
A worker refuses to reach into equipment that could restart automatically and follows the energy-control procedure.
commonMistakes: Assuming simple-looking equipment cannot contain hazardous energy.
Disassembling equipment because the repair seems easy.
content.practicalApplication: Review maintenance scenarios and mark the exact point where routine operator care ends and authorized servicing begins.
content.summary: Technician I workers support reliability through assigned routine care while escalating disassembly, protected access and hazardous-energy servicing to authorized personnel.

blocks.title: Operator care is a defined assignment, not a sliding scale
blocks.body: Accessible cleaning, observation, setup, simple checks, or consumable replacement may belong to the operator only when the equipment instructions and facility SOP assign those actions. A task does not become operator care simply because it appears mechanically simple or because the technician has performed similar repairs elsewhere.

blocks.alt: Two-column visual distinguishing explicitly assigned routine operator care from servicing and technical maintenance that may involve guards, hazardous motion, protected electrical components, powered disassembly, pressure, stored energy, or other hazards requiring the employer-defined authorized role.
blocks.caption: Use the controlled operator procedure to find the boundary. Do not move the boundary yourself because the next step looks easy.

blocks.title: The same symptom can lead to different authority boundaries

left.label: Within operator procedure
left.body: An irrigation emitter is checked externally using the assigned operator method. The observable condition is recorded, and the defined simple operator action is completed if the SOP explicitly allows it.

right.label: Servicing boundary
right.body: The blockage can only be reached by disassembling a powered component or entering an area with unexpected startup or stored-energy risk. The technician stops and refers the condition to the authorized servicing process.

blocks.title: Signals that the job may have crossed into servicing
rows: Guard or protective cover must be removed
May expose hazardous motion or protected components
Stop at the operator boundary and refer under procedure
Do not reach in; use the employer's energy-control process
Pressure, gravity, heat, mechanical force, or other stored energy must be released
Unexpected energy release can injure workers
Do not expand routine operator care into energy-control work
The manual/SOP does not assign the action to the operator
Stop and clarify rather than improvise

blocks.title: A jam appears easy to reach
blocks.setting: Material is visibly jammed just inside a guarded area. The equipment has stopped, but it can restart automatically after a fault clears. The operator SOP does not authorize reaching past the guard.
options: Reach in quickly while the equipment is stopped
Hold the stop button while another worker removes the material
Stop at the operator-care boundary and follow the authorized servicing/energy-control process
Remove the guard because the jam is visible
blocks.answer: Stop at the operator-care boundary and follow the authorized servicing/energy-control process.
blocks.feedback: A stopped condition is not proof that hazardous energy is controlled. The action requires protected access beyond the assigned operator procedure.

blocks.title: Find the exact boundary
blocks.instructions: Review equipment-care scenarios and mark the last action that remains inside the supplied operator procedure and the first action that requires maintenance or another authorized role.
prompts: Visible hose inspection becomes internal pump access.
Operator reset becomes repeated reset of an unresolved fault.
Consumable replacement becomes exposure to a protected electrical component.
Routine jam observation becomes guarded-area entry.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Routine care supports equipment reliability. It does not grant hazardous-energy, electrical, mechanical, or skilled-maintenance authority. When the controlled operator procedure ends, competent performance is to stop and refer the work.
